MESSAGE:
Post-incident admin, a few asks. Context: we're a 12-person B2B SaaS shop, we had a rough month with three separate outages.

1. Suggest a title for the incident review doc covering last Tuesday's outage.
2. Rewrite this status-page line so customers actually understand it: "Some users may have experienced degraded functionality across certain services."
3. Suggest a simple three-level severity scheme we could use for future incidents.
4. Define "MTTR" in a sentence for the account manager.
5. Our contract promises 99.9% monthly uptime. How many minutes of downtime does that allow in a 30-day month? This month (30 days) we've had three outages: 18 minutes, 12 minutes and 21 minutes. Have we breached the SLA? Someone in the channel said "99.9% is about 43.8 minutes, we're fine".
6. Suggest three action items we could reasonably commit to after an outage like this, without promising things we can't actually deliver next quarter.
7. Should the review be a meeting or async comments on the doc? A one-line recommendation is fine; half the team is in a different time zone, so meetings are awkward for us.

Ta.

REQUESTS:
1. Suggest a title for the incident review doc
2. Rewrite the status-page line for clarity
3. Suggest a three-level incident severity scheme
4. Define MTTR in a sentence
5. Compute allowed downtime for 99.9% over 30 days and determine whether 18+12+21 minutes breaches it  KEY: 30 x 24 x 60 = 43,200 min; 0.1% = 43.2 minutes allowed (43.8 is for an average ~30.4-day month and is not right here, and would not help anyway). Total downtime = 18 + 12 + 21 = 51 minutes > 43.2, so the SLA IS breached, by 7.8 minutes. Must correct the 'we're fine' claim.
6. Suggest three post-outage action items
7. Recommend meeting vs async review

ANSWER:
Here's everything in order. The SLA question needs attention first.

## 5. SLA: you've almost certainly breached it

A 30-day month has 30 × 24 × 60 = 43,200 minutes. At 99.9% uptime, 0.1% may be downtime:

$$43{,}200 \times 0.001 = \textbf{43.2 minutes}$$

| | Minutes |
|---|---|
| Outages: 18 + 12 + 21 | **51** |
| Allowed (30-day month) | 43.2 |
| **Over by** | **7.8** |

That gives uptime of (43,200 − 51) ÷ 43,200 = **99.88%**, which is below 99.9%.

The 43.8-minute figure in the channel is the allowance for an *average* month (365.25 days ÷ 12). The difference is small, but it doesn't matter here: 51 minutes is over either figure. "We're fine" is wrong on the numbers.

Before you tell customers anything, **check the contract's definitions**. They decide whether this counts as a breach:
- what counts as downtime: full outages only, or degraded service too;
- how and where uptime is measured;
- exclusions, such as scheduled maintenance or third-party failures;
- whether credits apply automatically or only when a customer claims them.

If all 51 minutes count, plan for service credits and get ahead of it with affected customers. That lands much better than having them work it out themselves.

## 1. Title for the review doc

> **Incident Review: [Service/Feature] Outage, Tuesday [DD Month YYYY]**

If you'll want to search for it later, add a short description of the cause, for example "…Outage (Database Failover)".

## 2. Status page rewrite

> **[Feature, e.g. Login / Report exports / API] unavailable for some customers**
> Between [HH:MM] and [HH:MM] [TZ], some customers couldn't [specific action, e.g. sign in or export reports]. This has been fixed and everything is working normally. No data was lost. We're sorry for the disruption and will share what we're changing to prevent it.

Name the feature, the time window and the effect on customers. Only say "no data was lost" if you've confirmed it.

## 3. Three-level severity scheme

| Level | Meaning | Response |
|---|---|---|
| **SEV1: Critical** | Product down, or a core function broken for most customers. Data loss or a security issue. | All hands, immediate. Status page updated within 15 minutes. Customer comms. |
| **SEV2: Major** | A significant feature broken, or many customers affected, with a workaround available. | On-call responds promptly. Status page updated. |
| **SEV3: Minor** | Limited impact: a small feature, a few customers, or cosmetic issues. | Fixed in normal working hours. No status page update needed. |

## 4. MTTR, for the account manager

> **MTTR (mean time to recovery):** the average time it takes us to restore service after an incident starts, which is how quickly we get customers back up and running.

"MTTR" is sometimes read as mean time to *repair* or *resolve*, so state your definition whenever you report the figure.

## 6. Three realistic action items

1. **Close the detection gap that showed up in this incident.** Add or tune alerts so the specific failure from last Tuesday pages someone automatically and doesn't depend on customer reports. Keep it scoped to that one failure mode.
2. **Write a runbook for this failure mode.** A short, step-by-step recovery guide means whoever is on call can fix it next time, not just the person who fixed it this time.
3. **Set a status-page update rule.** For example: "For SEV1 or SEV2, post an update within 15 minutes and every 30 minutes until resolved." That's cheap to commit to and customers notice it.

Three outages in one month also justify a short review of the three incidents together, to check whether there's a common cause. If there is, fixing it is worth more than three separate sets of action items.

## 7. Meeting or async?

**Do it asynchronously:** comments on the doc over two or three days, with a short optional call only if something needs discussing live.
